idiom_name: hand-written conversion functions per direction in one mapping translation unit (struct -> struct)
implementation_notes: C has no reflection and no mapping facility, so the mapper is a pair of functions in one translation unit: `int user_from_dto(const struct user_dto *in, struct user *out)` and `int user_to_dto(const struct user *in, struct user_dto *out)`, each copying field by field and translating types, units and absent-value conventions (a null pointer or a sentinel member). Keeping both directions in the same file - with the DTO header included nowhere else - is what makes the mapping reviewable and keeps the two layouts independent. Return an error code (or bool plus out-parameter) instead of skipping a field silently, and state string ownership explicitly (borrowed versus copied, who frees). Use a struct of function pointers (an ops table) only when several wire formats must sit behind one mapper interface; for a fixed pair of structs, plain functions are the honest form.
pitfalls: The compiler sees no relation between the two structs: adding a member to the DTO leaves the mapper stale and the field silently zero, so mapping needs its own tests.
A conversion that returns the target struct by value copies fixed buffers but not the ownership rule of a malloc'd member - decide who frees and say so in the header.
Casting between differently sized or signed members (int32 DTO id versus uint64 domain id) is where truncation and sign-extension bugs live; convert explicitly and range-check.
Reading a struct that the mapper partially filled is silent undefined behaviour: either write every member or return an error before the caller sees the value.
